#1PLMRPalomar Holdings, Inc.BUY — a high-growth, debt-freeMEDIUMCORE▼

Endorsed by: 🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot + 🔄 Marks Second-Level + 💼 Goldman Sachs Small-Cap

Business: Palomar is a specialty P&C insurer underwriting catastrophe-exposed, hard-to-place risks (earthquake, inland flood, hurricane, surplus lines) that standard carriers avoid. It collects premiums on these niche perils and cedes most of the tail risk to reinsurers, keeping a capital-efficient, fee-like net economic profile while scaling its book. Its edge is underwriting expertise in underserved high-risk zones and disciplined reinsurance management, letting it grow premiums far faster than the broader insurance market.

Bull case: The financials are genuinely impressive: revenue grew 58% in 2025 to $876M (from $554M in 2024 and $248M in 2021), net income rose to $197M, and operating income hit $253M — a roughly 29% operating margin with a 5-year revenue CAGR above 35%. The balance sheet is pristine: essentially zero net debt with ~$100M net cash and ~$943M of equity, so this growth has been self-funded, not levered. Management just completed its June 1 reinsurance placement cleanly and RAISED full-year 2026 adjusted net income guidance to $266–280M, a strong signal that pricing and capacity remain favorable. Yet the stock is down 39% over the past year and sits near its 52-week low at ~$109, leaving it at ~15x trailing and only ~10x 2027 consensus EPS of ~$11 — a deep mismatch between operating momentum and price. If Palomar simply continues compounding premiums and avoids an outsized cat year, the multiple should re-rate meaningfully.

Bear case: This is structurally a catastrophe-exposed insurer — one major earthquake, hurricane or flood season can produce a quarter that erases a year of disciplined gains, and reinsurance only caps, not eliminates, that risk. The screener's eye-popping PEG of 0.26 and +51% DCF margin of safety lean entirely on trailing hypergrowth (58%) that is mathematically decelerating; analyst forward EPS estimates ($11 in 2027, $12 in 2028) imply low-double-digit growth, not 58%, so the cheap-PEG narrative overstates the case. Most tellingly, consensus price target is $110.25 (median $109.50) versus a $109.32 price — the Street sees essentially ZERO upside, contradicting the DCF's $222 intrinsic value. Coverage is thin (only 1–3 analysts on out-year estimates), insider activity is purely routine board stock awards with no open-market buying, and the stock fell 9% post-earnings despite a record quarter — suggesting the market is repricing forward growth, not the past.

Valuation: Mixed. On trailing earnings it looks cheap (~15x P/E, FCF yield 12%) and on forward 2027 EPS of ~$11 it's only ~10x — attractive for a 30%+ historical grower. But the DCF intrinsic value of $222 (+51% MoS) and PEG of 0.26 are flattered by unsustainable trailing growth, and the analyst consensus PT of ~$110 implies the stock is roughly fairly valued at today's price. My rough fair-value view: ~$140–160 if growth normalizes to ~15% with no major cat loss (≈12–14x forward EPS) — meaningful upside, but well short of the $222 DCF. Call it undervalued by ~25–40%, not 51%.

Catalysts: The raised 2026 adjusted NI guidance ($266–280M) and clean June 1 reinsurance placement are immediate positives that the market hasn't priced. Q2 2026 earnings (expected late July/early August) showing continued premium growth and a benign loss ratio could drive a re-rate. Recent acquisition integration, further specialty-line expansion, and rising investment income (a tailwind with the 10Y at 4.55%) are additional levers.

What to watch (4–12 wks): Q2 2026 earnings (~late July/Aug) — watch gross written premium growth, net combined ratio, and any further guidance revision. Track whether thin analyst estimates get revised UP after the guidance raise (a key re-rating signal). Monitor the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and any cat-loss disclosures (8-K). Watch for any shift from routine board awards to open-market insider BUYING, which would meaningfully raise conviction.

Time horizon: 2-3 years to let premium compounding and a multiple re-rate play out, with the Q2 print and hurricane season as near-term 3-6 month checkpoints.

#2QLYSQualys, Inc.WATCH — exceptional quality anMEDIUMCORE▼

Endorsed by: 🔄 Marks Second-Level + 👁️ Insider & 13F Tracker + 🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared

Business: Qualys is a pure-play cloud-based cybersecurity platform focused on vulnerability management, compliance/policy monitoring, and attack surface management — a continuous scanner telling enterprises and government agencies where their security holes are across IT, cloud and OT estates. Revenue is almost entirely recurring SaaS subscription, sold to large enterprises and the public sector with deep workflow integrations. It is asset-light (no on-prem hardware), highly profitable, and competes against Tenable, Rapid7, and increasingly the broader platforms of CrowdStrike, Microsoft and Wiz that are bundling exposure-management into wider security suites.

Bull case: This is a textbook quietly-compounding software franchise. FY25 revenue of $669M grew ~10% (vs ~10% in FY24 and ~12% in FY23), with operating income of $222M (33% operating margin) and net income of $198M — and crucially these margins are expanding, not just holding (operating income up from $130M in 2022 to $222M in 2025). The balance sheet is a genuine fortress: $250M cash against $97M debt for ~$153M net cash, and equity has grown every year. Returns on capital near 29% and FCF margins north of 40% mean the business self-funds buybacks while compounding. Mandatory, non-discretionary demand (vulnerability management is required by regulation and cyber-insurance) gives recurring-revenue durability through downturns, and the at-17.6x trailing P/E valuation for a 29% ROIC, net-cash compounder is undemanding relative to security-software peers that trade at multiples of this. Continued margin expansion plus modest buybacks could drive low-teens EPS growth even on high-single-digit revenue.

Bear case: The core risk is that Qualys is a great business in a maturing, increasingly contested niche. Revenue growth has settled into the ~10% range and analyst forward estimates imply deceleration — consensus models only ~$825M of revenue by 2028 and ~$950M by 2029, i.e. high-single-digit growth, not the 15%+ that would justify premium re-rating. Vulnerability management is being absorbed into broader exposure-management and CNAPP platforms by CrowdStrike, Wiz/Google, Microsoft and Tenable, threatening Qualys's standalone relevance and pricing power. The screener's DCF intrinsic value of $304.94 implies ~180% upside, which is wildly inconsistent with its own stated +64% margin of safety and with the analyst price-target consensus of just $103 (median $100, high $125) — that DCF is not credible and should be discounted. After a ~23% post-earnings run to ~$108, the stock now sits essentially at consensus fair value with insiders (CEO Thakar and others) trimming. Limited analyst coverage (4-9 estimates) also means thin institutional support if growth disappoints.

Valuation: Fairly-to-fully valued, not deeply cheap. At $108 and 17.6x trailing P/E with ~8% FCF yield, it's reasonably priced for a 29%-ROIC net-cash compounder — but the most reliable anchors disagree with the screener's bullish framing. Analyst PT consensus is $103 (median $100), i.e. the stock is trading slightly ABOVE consensus fair value after its rally. On forward EPS (~$8.7 for 2028, ~$10.1 for 2029), it trades ~12-13x 2028 earnings — fair for high-single-digit growth, not a bargain. I'd treat the $304.94 DCF as unreliable; a defensible fair-value range is roughly $100-120, putting the current price near the middle. PEG ~1.08 reinforces 'fairly valued.'

Catalysts: Next quarterly earnings (Q2 FY26, expected late July/early August) with calibrated guidance and net revenue retention/billings trends; new product traction in attack-surface management and TotalCloud/CNAPP that could re-accelerate growth; large federal/government contract wins given its FedRAMP positioning; resumption or acceleration of buybacks; and any M&A interest given its net-cash balance sheet and strategic-asset profile in a consolidating security market.

What to watch (4–12 wks): Q2 FY26 earnings date and whether revenue growth holds ~10% or slips toward high-single digits; the direction of analyst estimate revisions (currently thin coverage); billings and net dollar retention disclosure; product milestones in exposure/attack-surface management; and insider activity — recent CEO and officer sales are small/routine but a shift to cluster buying or larger sales is worth tracking. Also watch the ~23% post-earnings momentum for mean-reversion if the next print is merely in-line.

Time horizon: 3-5 years for the quiet-compounder thesis to pay off; near-term it's a WATCH with a buy-the-dip stance below ~$95 where margin of safety improves.

#3ATATAtour Lifestyle Holdings LimitedBUY — a genuinely high-qualityMEDIUMSATELLITE▼

Endorsed by: 🛒 Lynch Buy What You Know + 📱 Camillo Social Arbitrage

Business: Atour operates and franchises design-forward 'lifestyle' hotels across mainland China under the Atour and Atour S brands, targeting urban business and leisure travellers aged 25-45. Its model is largely asset-light (manachised/franchised), so it earns high-margin management fees while franchisees fund the capex; on top of that it runs a fast-scaling retail segment selling branded sleep products (mattresses, pillows, bedding) that guests sample in-room — a clever 'try-then-buy' funnel now approaching ~a third of revenue. The combination of recurring fee income plus a viral consumer-products flywheel gives it structurally higher returns on capital than a traditional hotel owner.

Bull case: The financials confirm a rare compounder: revenue rose from ¥2.26B (2022) to ¥4.67B (2023) to ¥7.25B (2024) to ¥9.79B (2025), with net income scaling from ¥98M to ¥1.62B over the same span — operating margin expanded from ~7% to ~24% and gross margin sits near 44-48%, evidence of real operating leverage as the network densifies. The balance sheet is fortress-like: ~¥3.3B cash against ¥1.5B debt for net cash of ~¥1.78B RMB (note: roughly US$245M, not US$1.78B), funding expansion without dilution. The asset-light model drives high ROIC (~31%), and the retail engine — where management recently raised FY26 retail topline guidance by ~5pp — adds a second growth vector decoupled from room counts. At ~18x trailing earnings against 35% revenue growth (PEG <0.8), this is a Lynchian 'fast grower at a value price' with 11-12 analysts at a $45 consensus target implying ~34% upside, plus a sell-side floor of fresh BUY notes ($45-50 targets).

Bear case: This is a China consumer ADR, so it carries the full discount stack: ADR/VIE structure and delisting/audit risk, RMB depreciation eroding USD-reported returns, and a soft Chinese consumer and travel-spend backdrop that could compress ADR/RevPAR and slow franchise signings. Growth is decelerating (from triple-digit reopening rebounds toward +35%), and the law of large numbers plus rising hotel-count saturation in tier-1/2 cities will keep pressuring the rate of expansion. The retail segment, while exciting, is increasingly the swing factor — a single-product (sleep goods) consumer line is fashion- and competition-sensitive and could disappoint against raised guidance. Insider data shows no recent cluster buying (mostly routine/option-related activity), and the screener's headline claims are unreliable: the touted '$1.78B net cash,' '$225 DCF intrinsic value / +85% margin of safety,' and 'zero analyst coverage' are all wrong (RMB-vs-USD confusion and stale data), so anyone underwriting those numbers is mispricing the risk.

Valuation: Reasonably valued-to-modestly-cheap, not the 85%-discount the screener implies. Ignore the $225 DCF and 'zero coverage' figures — they are artifacts of mixing RMB financials with a USD ADR price. The honest anchors: ~18x TTM P/E on ~35% growth (PEG ~0.7-0.8) is attractive for a high-ROIC compounder, and consensus $45 target implies ~34% upside from $33.64. Forward estimates (analysts model continued double-digit revenue growth toward ~¥15B in 2027 and ~¥17.7B in 2028) support a fair-value range of roughly $42-50 if growth and margins hold — i.e., ~25-45% upside — while applying a China-ADR discount keeps a conservative fair value nearer $40.

Catalysts: Quarterly earnings (next print typically mid-to-late summer) showing sustained RevPAR and net-new-hotel growth; further upward revisions to FY26 retail guidance (management already raised it ~5pp); continued sell-side initiations/upgrades narrowing the gap to the $45 consensus; any capital-return move (buyback/dividend) given the net-cash balance sheet; and macro easing/stimulus supporting Chinese domestic travel.

What to watch (4–12 wks): Over the next 4-12 weeks: (1) the next quarterly 6-K — watch hotel-count net adds, RevPAR/ADR/occupancy trend, and retail GMV growth versus the raised FY26 guide; (2) direction of analyst estimate revisions and whether targets cluster above the current $45; (3) RMB/USD exchange rate (directly hits USD-reported results); (4) any insider open-market buying (so far none material); (5) China consumer/travel data points and any audit-oversight/delisting headlines affecting all US-listed China ADRs.

Time horizon: 2-3 years to let the hotel network and retail flywheel compound, with a 12-month catalyst path toward the $40-50 fair-value range.

Goldman Sachs pre-discovery screen — finding companies growing 25%+ in the $100M–$2B range before mainstream institutional flows arrive. Goal: tomorrow's $10B company at $500M today.

  • Size: $100M–$2B market cap — big enough to be legitimate, small enough to still multiply
  • Coverage: 0–5 analysts covering the stock (≥20 = already discovered)
  • Revenue growth: minimum 25% YoY for 3+ consecutive quarters
  • Insider ownership: founders/executives holding 15%+ of shares (skin in the game)
  • Structural tailwinds: AI, cybersecurity, energy transition, aging demographics, automation
  • Unit economics: improving gross margins and positive operating leverage (revenue growing faster than costs)
  • Balance sheet: 18+ months cash runway without needing profitability
  • Blindspot channels: spinoffs from S&P 500 companies, foreign listings overlooked by US investors, orphaned small-caps that fell below $500M and lost analyst coverage, post-bankruptcy equities with clean balance sheets
  • Near-term catalysts: specific re-rating events within 6–12 months (earnings beats, product launches, regulatory approvals)

Peter Lynch's everyday-life observation framework. Simple, understandable consumer and workplace businesses growing 15–25%/yr at PEG <1.0. The best investments hide in plain sight — find them before Wall Street does.

  • Daily life inventory: products, apps, or services you're using more this year than last year

  • Lynch category: classify each as Fast Grower (20%+ growth), Stalwart, Cyclical, Turnaround, or Asset Play
  • The 'so what' test: a popular product doesn't automatically make a great stock — always check valuation and fundamentals

Christopher Mayer's 100-Bagger framework — the research methodology identifying stocks with potential to return 100x, based on patterns observed across 365 historical 100-baggers.

  • Small starting cap: ideally under $1B — 100x must be mathematically possible
  • Long runway: serves a market large enough to support decades of revenue growth

  • No dilution: the company isn't issuing large amounts of new shares that erode long-term returns
  • Twin engines test: can earnings grow 10x AND the P/E multiple also expand to compound into 100x?
  • Time horizon reality: 100-baggers typically take 20–25 years — patience is the edge

🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula — 2 picks ▼
🔢 Greenblatt Magic Formula
Joel Greenblatt's two-factor screen: ROIC >20% AND earnings yield >10%. Pre-filtered candidate pool; agent secondarily filters for sustainability and earnings quality.
📖 Strategy details▼

Joel Greenblatt's Magic Formula — the two-factor screen generating 30%+ annual returns over 20 years by finding companies that are simultaneously high-quality AND cheap.

  • ROIC above 20%: high-quality business generating strong returns on every dollar invested
  • Earnings yield above 10%: cheap relative to earnings (inverse of P/E) — the 'cheap' gate
  • Combined ranking: companies score best when BOTH metrics rank highly — quality + cheap together
  • Size filter: $50M–$10B to exclude illiquid micro-caps and already-covered mega-caps
  • Sector exclusions: skip financials, utilities, and REITs (different capital structures distort the formula)
  • Debt check: high ROIC shouldn't be mere financial leverage — verify balance sheet is clean
  • Earnings quality: free cash flow should match net income — flag accounting-driven earnings
  • Temporary vs permanent: is the stock cheap due to a fixable problem, or is the business structurally declining?

🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet — 4 picks ▼
🎲 Pabrai Asymmetric Bet
Mohnish Pabrai's 3:1+ upside/downside framework. Downside protected by real assets or cash; upside driven by a specific catalyst the market is underpricing.
📖 Strategy details▼

Mohnish Pabrai's Dhandho framework — combining LOW RISK (limited downside) with HIGH UNCERTAINTY (Wall Street can't value it) for asymmetric bets where heads I win big, tails I don't lose much.

  • Asymmetry ratio: upside potential ÷ downside risk must be 3:1 or better
  • Downside protection: what specifically limits the loss — asset value, cash, acquisition target, recurring revenue
  • Upside catalyst: the specific event that could drive 3–10x returns over 3–5 years
  • Temporary distress: markets treating a short-term problem (lawsuit, earnings miss, sector rotation) as permanent
  • Special situations: spinoffs, post-bankruptcy equities, rights offerings that create pricing inefficiencies
  • Hated industries: entire sectors abandoned by investors where survivors trade at distressed multiples
  • Margin of safety: gap between current price and conservative intrinsic value — the buffer against being wrong

🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared — 4 picks ▼
🌀 Sleep Scale Economics Shared
Nick Sleep's flywheel framework — businesses that share scale benefits with customers (Costco/Amazon model), driving self-reinforcing growth as they scale.
📖 Strategy details▼

Nick Sleep's Scale Economics Shared framework — the methodology that identified Amazon, Costco, and Berkshire decades early, based on companies that share their scale advantages with customers to build a self-reinforcing flywheel.

  • Core test: does the company get MORE efficient and offer BETTER prices as it grows? (opposite of most businesses)
  • Customer obsession: willing to take short-term margin hits to give customers more value (Costco 15% margin discipline)
  • Flywheel: lower prices → more customers → more scale → lower costs → even lower prices (self-reinforcing loop)
  • Long-term thinking evidence: quarterly earnings suppressed for multi-year investment; founder letters emphasise decades
  • Customer lifetime value: expanding over time as the business creates more value per customer
  • Non-obvious moat: the advantage isn't patents or brand — it's a culture and business model the organisation embodies
  • Capital allocation: cash flow reinvested into high-return opportunities rather than buybacks at peak prices

Michael Burry's catalyst-driven deep value approach — finding mispriced assets where specific, identifiable catalysts will force the market to recognise hidden value within a defined timeframe.

  • Hidden assets: companies trading below the value of real estate, cash, or investments on the balance sheet
  • Sum-of-parts: conglomerates where individual divisions are worth more than the combined market cap
  • Activist catalyst: stocks where an activist could force a spinoff, sale, or restructuring to unlock value
  • Regulatory / legal catalysts: upcoming court cases or policy decisions that will materially reprice the stock
  • Balance sheet transformation: companies paying down debt aggressively — will re-rate once leverage drops below key thresholds
  • Accounting normalisation: one-time write-downs or unusual items temporarily depressing reported earnings
  • Catalyst timeline: each idea must have a specific catalyst with 6–18 month resolution — no 'cheap forever' open-ended theses

🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot — 3 picks ▼
🛰️ Wall Street Blindspot
Finds investment opportunities Wall Street's major banks can't or won't cover — coverage gaps, spinoffs, orphaned names, sin-sector discounts, IPO aftermath.
📖 Strategy details▼

Wall Street Blindspot framework — finding investment opportunities that major banks structurally cannot or will not cover: coverage gaps, orphaned names, stigmatised sectors, complex structures.

  • Coverage gap: companies with 0–5 sell-side analysts — institutions only cover above $2B, leaving quality names persistently mispriced
  • Orphaned mid-caps: companies that fell below $500M and lost coverage — often trading at deep discounts to intrinsic value
  • Spinoff aftermath: newly independent companies facing forced selling from index funds in the first 18 months
  • Sin-sector discounts: quality companies in gambling, tobacco, fossil fuels, or defence at persistent ESG mandate discounts
  • Post-bankruptcy emergence: restructured balance sheets institutional investors can't own due to mandate restrictions
  • IPO aftermath: quality companies 18–24 months post-IPO when lockup expiry creates selling pressure
  • Key signal: the discount reason is structural or temporary, not fundamental — the business is better than the price suggests

🏢 About
Palomar is a specialty insurance company focused exclusively on catastrophe-exposed, hard-to-place risks that standard carriers avoid — earthquakes, inland flood, hurricane, and surplus lines. It earns premiums by underwriting these niche perils, then buys reinsurance to cap its net exposure, keeping the asset-light fee-like economics while growing its book. Its customers are homeowners, businesses, and agricultural operators in high-risk zones underserved by mainstream insurers.
Industry: Specialty Catastrophe Insurance · vs: Kingsway Financial, RLI Corp, Skyward Specialty Insurance

"Palomar is the most structurally misunderstood name in this entire universe. It sits in Financial Services — a sector that's genuinely cheap (sector PEG 1.0, FCF yield 7.2%) — yet PLMR itself has been hammered 39% over the past year despite just posting its strongest quarter ever in absolute earnings terms. Revenue compound from $248M in 2021 to $876M in 2025 with operating income exploding from $57M to $253M; this is not a stumbling business, it's a business the market is re-rating lower because 'catastrophe insurer' gets lumped with climate-tail-risk anxiety. The no-analyst coverage (zero sell-side initiations) means there is literally no institutional voice correcting this misperception. The DCF margin of safety is 51% and the PEG is 0.3 — extraordinarily cheap for a company compounding operating income at roughly 45% per year. The June 1 reinsurance placement was just completed successfully and full-year 2026 adjusted net income guidance was raised to $266–280M against a $2.9B market cap — that's a sub-11x forward earnings multiple on a specialty franchise that has never been available this cheap. At 62% of its 52-week high with fresh guidance upside, the entry feels genuinely asymmetric."

The market is pricing Palomar as a disaster-risk liability rather than as a disciplined, asset-light specialty insurer compounding earnings at 40%+ per year with zero sell-side coverage to correct the narrative.
